questions.question: A man with a kidney transplant sustained a small finger wound at a lake house and developed a worsening purulent skin and soft-tissue infection despite multiple courses of antibiotics. Bacterial cultures are negative, no acid-fast bacilli are seen, and a few white yeast-like colonies on Sabouraud media were discarded as presumed contaminants. A periodic acid-Schiff stain of the lesion shows a morula-like "soccer ball" organism. questions.question_raw: Man with kidney transplant had a recent small finger wound at a lake house. Worsening purulent SSTI despite multiple courses of antibiotics. Picture of hand with a purulent ulceration or two.Bacterial cultures negative, no acid-fast bacilli seen. There were a few white yeast-like colonies growing on Sabourad media, but they were thought to be contaminants and discarded. Shown below is the result of a periodic acid-Schiff stain of the lesion, demonstrating a morula-like “soccer ball” organism. (It’s protothecosis, apparently; I googled it after coming home. WTF.) To what group does this organism belong?
What are two treatments for it?

questions.model_answer: a) Prototheca (most commonly Prototheca wickerhamii). b) It is an achlorophyllous (colorless) unicellular green alga; the pathognomonic PAS-positive endosporulating sporangium gives the "morula"/soccer-ball appearance. c) (1) Surgical debridement/excision combined with systemic antifungal therapy. (2) Amphotericin B, or an azole such as itraconazole (tetracyclines have also been used adjunctively); reduction of immunosuppression should be pursued where possible.
questions.beyond_mandell: Protothecosis is not covered in the Harmful Algal Blooms chapter; answer drawn from Mandell's algae/Prototheca material and standard ID references.

questions.question: A woman who had a liver transplant 8 months ago sustained an arm injury at a cottage and now has an ulcer without lymphangitis. Staining of a sample shows "soccer ball"-like morulas. The isolate grows on Sabouraud agar within 7 days with yeast-like colonies, but the technologist discarded it before workup. Blood and wound cultures are negative and no acid-fast bacilli are seen.
questions.question_raw: A patient had a liver transplant 8 months ago. She has an injury to her R arm while at a cottage. Now has an ulcer with no lymphangitis. On staining from a sample, there are 'soccer ball' like morulas. The isolate grows on SAB within 7 days and colonies look like yeast morphologically, but the tech throws it out before working up. Blood and wound culture negative. No AFB.
questions.model_answer: a) Prototheca (typically Prototheca wickerhamii). b) Family Chlorellaceae (achlorophyllous green algae). c) (1) Surgical debridement/excision. (2) Amphotericin B or an azole such as itraconazole (± adjunctive tetracycline), with reduction of immunosuppression where feasible.
questions.beyond_mandell: Protothecosis is not covered in the Harmful Algal Blooms chapter; answer drawn from standard Mandell/ID references.

cohort_answer.text: a) Prototheca. b) Chlorellaceae. c) Surgical debridement; Ampho B + tetracycline OR oral azole (e.g. itraconazole).

questions.model_answer: (1) Paralytic shellfish poisoning – saxitoxin (Alexandrium spp.; associated with red tides). (2) Neurotoxic shellfish poisoning – brevetoxins (Karenia brevis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciguatera (ciguatoxin, Gambierdiscus) is an equally acceptable answer but its detailed description falls outside this text slice.

cohort_answer.text: Ciguatera Fish Poisoning: toxin Ciguatoxin, formed by dinoflagellates of the genus Gambierdiscus (single-cell algae growing on coral reefs). Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning: toxin Saxitoxin, caused by ingestion of bivalve mollusks (mussels, clams, scallops, oysters) and crabs/snails contaminated with dinoflagellates of the genus Alexandrium (associated with red tides); symptoms within hours - perioral tingling, ataxia, difficulty swallowing, dizziness, paresthesias, weakness, paralysis, brainstem dysfunction, respiratory failure. Neurotoxic Shellfish Poisoning: ingestion of shellfish contaminated by Karenia brevis (formerly Gymnodinium breve, associated with red tides); GI distress and neurologic symptoms (paresthesias of face/mouth/extremities, dizziness, ataxia, muscle aches, temperature-related dysesthesia, seizures); symptoms typically resolve within 3 days.
